title: Achieving perfect completeness for one- and two-message quantum proof systems
abstract: While quantum interactive proof systems using at least three messages can achieve perfect completeness, as shown by Kitaev and Watrous (STOC 2000), whether perfect completeness is achievable for one- and two-message quantum proof systems has remained open. For the one-message case, whether $\sf QMA$ can achieve perfect completeness was posed as an open problem in Watrous (FOCS 2000) and Aharonov and Naveh (2002); for the two-message case, the corresponding problems were (implicitly) posed in Jain, Upadhyay, and Watrous~(FOCS 2009) and Kobayashi, Le Gall, and Nishimura (SICOMP, 2019).   In this work, we establish that ${\sf QIP}(2)$, ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$, $\sf QAM$, and $\sf QMA$ can achieve perfect completeness. Here ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$ denotes the class of promise problems admitting two-message quantum-public-coin quantum interactive proof systems in which the verifier's only message consists of half-EPR pairs. Our main technical contributions are the follows:   1. For $\sf QMA$ (and directly for $\sf QAM$), an exactly constructible block-encoded matrix whose kernel certifies yes instances, constructed from the acceptance operator induced by the verification circuit.   2. For ${\sf QIP}(2)$ (and implicitly ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$), a new turn-halving transformation that preserves completeness and ensures that the resulting proof system retains at least two messages, provided that the terminal state before the final measurement is efficiently preparable.
summary: This paper resolves long-standing open problems regarding the perfect completeness of one- and two-message quantum proof systems like QMA and QIP(2). The authors achieve this by developing new mathematical tools, including a novel 'turn-halving transformation' and constructing specific certifying matrices. This work deepens the understanding of the computational power achievable in restricted quantum verification protocols.
main_problem: The paper addresses the open question of whether perfect completeness can be achieved for quantum interactive proof systems involving only one or two messages.
main_result: The authors establish that the classes QIP(2), qq-QAM, QAM, and QMA can all achieve perfect completeness under specific constructions.
method: The techniques involve constructing exactly constructible block-encoded matrices for QMA/QAM and introducing a new 'endpoint-inward turn-halving transformation' for QIP(2)/qq-QAM.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum interactive proof systems (QIP), where a quantum verifier interacts with a prover, characterized by message count (one or two messages) and the concept of perfect completeness (acceptance probability of 1 for yes instances).
key_observables: Completeness (probability of acceptance for yes instances, aiming for 1) and Soundness (maximum acceptance probability for no instances).
important_parameters: Message count (1 or 2), the specific quantum complexity classes (QMA, QAM, QIP(2)), and the error bounds derived from matrix properties (e.g., $1 - 2^{-16}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of specific label structures and the ability to construct polynomial-size, exact unitary operators ($U_K$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates two types of turn-halving transformations, contrasting the known 'middle-outward' method with the newly proposed 'endpoint-inward' transformation.
paper_structure: The paper systematically proves perfect completeness for the various restricted quantum proof systems by applying novel transformations and matrix constructions, culminating in explicit bounds for both completeness and soundness.
why_interesting: While the focus is on complexity theory, the techniques involving state preparation, entanglement manipulation, and precise probability bounding are highly relevant to understanding the limits of quantum communication protocols and quantum channel characterization.
